query: How can melting temperature, enthalpy and entropy of fusion, volume change at melting, and liquid-phase thermodynamic properties be determined accurately and efficiently across the high-entropy-alloy family? State the physical rationale, expected quantitative performance, range of applicability, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive validation result that would rule out the proposed approach.

generation.hypothesis: Advanced CALPHAD modeling, when extended with high-throughput assessments and refined thermodynamic parameters from well‐characterized binary and ternary subsystems, can accurately predict the melting temperature, fusion enthalpy and entropy, volume change upon melting, and liquid-phase thermodynamic properties across the high-entropy-alloy family.
generation.material_initial_state: Solid solution high-entropy alloys (HEAs) with compositions within well-assessed binary/ternary subsystems.
generation.intervention: Develop and apply a high-throughput CALPHAD framework that integrates both experimental inputs (e.g., DSC, calorimetry) and theoretically computed thermodynamic parameters to construct a comprehensive database covering liquid and solid phases.
generation.conditions: Applicable for HEAs whose compositions lie within the range of available thermodynamic data (e.g., systems where >50% of binary interactions have been characterized) and temperatures spanning from room temperature up to and beyond the melting point.
generation.structural_mediator: The phase equilibria and Gibbs free energy descriptions for competing phases (including the liquid phase) as mediated by configurational entropy, interatomic interactions, and volume effects at melting.
generation.mechanism: By accurately balancing contributions from fusion enthalpy and the corresponding entropy changes that determine the Gibbs free energy difference between solid and liquid phases, CALPHAD modeling can be used to determine the temperatures and latent heats of phase transition. Liquid-phase thermodynamics are modeled by extending these descriptions from binary/ternary systems to multicomponent HEAs, using systematically refined parameters.
generation.predicted_outcome: The approach is expected to predict melting temperatures, fusion enthalpy/entropy and volume changes at melting with quantitative accuracies within approximately 5–10% of experimental values, enabling efficient material screening and design across the HEA family.
generation.baseline: Traditional CALPHAD predictions based on incomplete database assessments often lack the resolution needed for accurate fusion property predictions in complex multi-component systems.
generation.boundary: This methodology is likely applicable only in composition ranges where sufficient experimental and theoretical data exist to calibrate the underlying thermodynamic models; predictions outside these ranges or for systems with poorly assessed binary/ternary interactions may have increased uncertainties.
generation.uncertainty: The level of accuracy depends on the completeness of the thermodynamic database for all relevant binary and ternary systems, and discrepancies may occur for systems with significant short-range ordering or minor phases not well-captured in the current databases.

falsification_experiment.design: Perform high-throughput differential scanning calorimetry (DSC) and drop calorimetry on a broad set of HEA compositions to measure melting temperature, fusion enthalpy/entropy, and volume change at melting. Independently, calculate these properties using the advanced CALPHAD approach. Compare the predictions to experimental findings over the complete assessed temperature range.
measurements: Fusion enthalpy and entropy via calorimetry
Volume change at melting via dilatometry or high-temperature density measurements
Liquid-phase thermodynamic parameters from phase equilibrium measurements
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If, over a statistically significant set of HEA compositions, the CALPHAD predictions deviate from the experimentally measured melting temperature, fusion enthalpy/entropy, and volume change by more than 10% or fail to capture key phase boundaries, then the proposed approach is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: The Gibbs free energy, G=H−TS, is the established thermodynamic criterion for phase selection, where H is enthalpy, S is entropy and T is absolute temperature. The Gibbs free energies for SS phases are described by enthalpies and entropies of mixing (Hmix and Smix), and IM phases are characterized by enthalpies and entropies of formation (Hf and Sf). The Gibbs free energies for all competing phases must be estimated, and the phase (or phases) with the lowest G gives the stable microstructure for that alloy. Smix, also called configurational entropy, is easy to modeland Hmix has been estimated for wide range of atom pairs. Sf for IM compounds is generally very small, and is often estimated to be zero. Hf of IM compounds is an essential term, but is difficult to estimate—there are no general models. Hmix is sometimes used as a proxy for Hf, but the differences between these values can be very large, and at best this approach gives only a relative ranking that cannot be used to determine G. The Calphad approach is used widely in the high entropy alloys and ceramics field [,,]. Senkov et al. demonstrated [] that for high entropy alloys, Calphad computations of type and number of phases agreed well with experimental results only when more than half of binary systems were fully assessed; however, even when there are enough data on binary and ternary systems, Calphad predictions of transformation temperatures, phase compositions and fractions are challenging. Compared with metals, the databases for oxides are much more limited, especially for the temperature range addressed in this study. Nevertheless, it is instructive to compare our experimental results with Calphad predictions.

The third-generation Gibbs energy expressions of pure Cr and V in both the liquid and A2 phases were established. By applying these expressions, the thermodynamic properties down to 0 K and thermal vacancy near the melting point can be well described. Besides, the lattice stability of Cr and V over the whole temperature range can be guaranteed. Based on the third-generation Gibbs energy expressions of pure elements, the Ta-Cr and Ta-V binary systems were thermodynamically assessed by considering the reviewed phase equilibria and thermodynamic data with the CALPHAD approach. A strategy to estimate the Gibbs energy of Laves phase was proposed by combining the theoretically computed and experimentally measured thermodynamic properties as well as semiempirical relation. Such a method was applied to C14 and C15 Laves phases in Ta-Cr and Ta-V binary systems. The calculated phase diagrams and thermodynamic properties showed nice agreement with the measured ones. Significant improvements can be observed at low temperatures compared with those from the second-generation thermodynamic descriptions, indicating the high reliability of the present thermodynamic descriptions.

chosen.approach: CALPHAD modeling for predicting fusion thermodynamics in alloys
